message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"4.16","text":"I will begin with the most kingly Zeus himself. His father Cronus swallowed his own children (as you say) and, with a sickle made of adamant, reaped off the genitals of his father Uranus; thus he showed those who emulate the mysteries of the gods the model of piety toward parents and affection toward children. Zeus himself bound his own father and confined him in Tartarus, and he punishes the other gods. For those who wish to practice unspeakable things, he fathered Metis and swallowed her. Metis, however, was seed, since it is impossible to swallow an infant. To provide a defense for pederasts, he abducts Ganymede. And, helping adulterers in defense of adultery, he himself repeatedly proves to be an adulterer. He urges people to commit incest with sisters by having intercourse with his sisters Hera and Demeter and with heavenly Aphrodite, whom some call Didone. For those who want to have intercourse with their daughters, by having intercourse with Persephone he becomes a wicked example from the myths. Indeed, he has committed countless impieties, so that, because of his surpassing lack of self-control, this abomination might be proclaimed a god by the impious.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"βασιλικωτάτου Διὸς","chosen":"the most kingly Zeus","rationale":"Preserves the emphatic superlative and the passage’s evident irony."},{"source_quote":"τὰ μόρια θερίσας","chosen":"reaped off the genitals","rationale":"Renders μόρια contextually as “genitals” while retaining the harvesting image of θερίζω."},{"source_quote":"ἀρρητουργεῖν","chosen":"to practice unspeakable things","rationale":"The verb denotes doing what cannot properly be spoken of; “commit abominations” is a possible stronger alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἦν δὲ ἡ Μῆτις γονή","chosen":"Metis, however, was seed","rationale":"γονή can mean generation, offspring, or reproductive seed. “Seed” best fits the following assertion that an infant could not be swallowed, though the statement remains deliberately strange."},{"source_quote":"ἀδελφοφθορεῖν","chosen":"to commit incest with sisters","rationale":"The compound denotes sexual violation or incest involving a sister, not literal destruction of a sibling."},{"source_quote":"Διδώνην","chosen":"Didone","rationale":"Transliterates the selected edition’s printed name rather than silently replacing it with the mythologically familiar Dione."},{"source_quote":"τὸ μύσος","chosen":"this abomination","rationale":"The contemptuous substantive characterizes Zeus himself as a source of defilement or abhorrence."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Διδώνην","issue":"The selected edition clearly reads Διδώνην, an unusual name here. The mythological context might suggest Dione, but the printed form remains intelligible as a name and has therefore been preserved as Didone.","proposed_reading":"Διώνην","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.17","text":"As for ordinary people, you could reasonably be moderately indignant about such notions; but as for those who proceed from education, what need is there even to speak? Some of them, claiming to be grammarians and sophists, affirm that deeds like these are worthy of gods. For since they themselves lack self-control, they seize on this mythical pretext and act brazenly while committing indecencies, as supposed imitators of their betters.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἰδιώταις","chosen":"ordinary people","rationale":"Here ἰδιῶται are people without specialized education, not “idiots” in the modern sense."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς δὲ ἐκ παιδείας ὁρμωμένοις","chosen":"as for those who proceed from education","rationale":"Retains the image of taking one’s point of departure from education; “those whose starting point is education” is an equivalent alternative."},{"source_quote":"γραμματικοὶ καὶ σοφισταὶ ἀξιοῦντες εἶναι","chosen":"claiming to be grammarians and sophists","rationale":"ἀξιοῦντες εἶναι expresses their claim to those learned designations rather than the narrator’s unqualified endorsement."},{"source_quote":"ὡς δὴ μιμηταὶ τῶν κρειττόνων","chosen":"as supposed imitators of their betters","rationale":"δή gives the claim an ironic or distancing force; κρείττονες denotes those regarded as superior."},{"source_quote":"παρρησιάζονται","chosen":"act brazenly","rationale":"The verb can mean speaking openly or behaving with bold freedom. The surrounding indecent conduct supports “act brazenly,” with “take liberties openly” as an alternative."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὰς τοιαύτας πράξεις θεῶν ἀξίας. εἶναι βεβαιοῦσιν","issue":"The printed full stop separates ἀξίας from the infinitive εἶναι that completes the construction. This is treated as editorial punctuation rather than missing or unreadable text, and the words are translated as continuous syntax.","proposed_reading":"τὰς τοιαύτας πράξεις θεῶν ἀξίας εἶναι βεβαιοῦσιν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.18","text":"For this reason, those who live in the countryside sin far less than those people do, since they have not been wickedly led in by the means through which those who dare these things were led in, having learned impiety from a bad education. For those who learn their letters from childhood through such myths, while the soul is still tender, cause the impious deeds of the so-called gods to grow into their own minds. Consequently, as their age increases, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul; and worst of all, the rooted impieties cannot easily be cut out, even when they are recognized as harmful by the people themselves once they have reached adulthood. For each person delights to remain in the things to which they have been habituated from childhood; and so, since habit is not much less powerful than nature, people become hard to turn toward good things that were not implanted in their souls from the beginning.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"αὐτῶν πολλῷ ἔλαττον","chosen":"far less than those people do","rationale":"The comparison most naturally refers to the educated defenders and imitators of the myths discussed immediately beforehand."},{"source_quote":"οὐκ εἰσηγμένοι πονηρῶς δι’ ὧν εἰσήχθησαν","chosen":"they have not been wickedly led in by the means through which ... were led in","rationale":"Preserves the repeated form of εἰσάγω. “Initiated” or “introduced” would also be possible, but might overstate a reference to formal mysteries."},{"source_quote":"μανθάνοντες γράμματα","chosen":"those who learn their letters","rationale":"γράμματα can refer to letters, reading, or literary education; the wording retains the elementary educational setting."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν αὑτῶν συνφύουσι νοῦν","chosen":"cause ... to grow into their own minds","rationale":"Preserves the organic image of συνφύω, which anticipates the subsequent language of seeds, roots, and fruit."},{"source_quote":"ὡς κακὰ σπέρματα καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ τελεσφοροῦσιν","chosen":"bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul","rationale":"τελεσφορέω describes reaching completion or bearing mature fruit; the agricultural rendering maintains the explicit seed image."},{"source_quote":"χαλεπὰ εἶναι νοῆται","chosen":"they are recognized as harmful","rationale":"χαλεπά may mean harmful, grievous, or difficult. “Harmful” suits the recognition that the ingrained practices are morally damaging; “recognized as grievous” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"τῆς συνηθείας οὐ πολὺ ἔλαττον πρὸς τὴν φύσιν δυναμένης","chosen":"habit is not much less powerful than nature","rationale":"Preserves the explicit comparison between the power of acquired habit and that of nature."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.19","text":"Therefore the young must not be trained in teachings that corrupt, and those in the prime of life must carefully guard themselves against listening to Greek mythology. For the teachings found among the Greeks are much worse than ignorance, as we have demonstrated from the fact that those living in the countryside sin less because they have not been educated in the teachings of the Greeks. One must therefore flee their myths of this sort, their theaters, and their books—if only it were possible, their cities too. For, filled with evil teachings and breathing something like madness upon those who vie with them, they pass on to their neighbors what they themselves have suffered. The worst thing is that whoever has received more education among them has been turned much farther away from thinking according to nature.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τοῖς διαφθείρουσιν ἀσκεῖσθαι μαθήμασιν","chosen":"be trained in teachings that corrupt","rationale":"ἀσκέω denotes disciplined training or practice, while the participle identifies the teachings by their corrupting effect."},{"source_quote":"ὑποστέλλεσθαι τῆς Ἑλλήνων ἐπακούειν μυθολογίας","chosen":"guard themselves against listening to Greek mythology","rationale":"The middle verb conveys drawing back or taking precautions; “shrink from hearing” is a more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"φευκτέον","chosen":"one must ... flee","rationale":"The verbal adjective expresses necessity, not merely advice to avoid the material."},{"source_quote":"πνέοντες τοῖς συναμιλλωμένοις ὥσπερ λύσσαν","chosen":"breathing something like madness upon those who vie with them","rationale":"λύσσα can denote raging madness, frenzy, or rabies. “Madness” preserves the image without restricting it to literal disease."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς συναμιλλωμένοις","chosen":"those who vie with them","rationale":"The participle denotes people striving or competing together; “those competing alongside them” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ... φρονεῖν ἐκτέτραπται","chosen":"has been turned ... away from thinking according to nature","rationale":"Retains the philosophical contrast between culturally acquired education and thought aligned with nature."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.20","text":"Some among them who even claim to be philosophers classify such offenses as matters of indifference and call those who are indignant at such practices foolish. For acts of this kind, they say, are not offenses by nature, but are things prohibited by enacted laws by sages who lived in the beginning, because those sages knew that people, readily agitated in soul and greatly distressed over such matters, go to war against one another. For this reason the sages established a law and prohibited such things as offenses. But it is ridiculous to suppose this. For how are things that cause disturbances, murders, and every kind of turmoil not offenses? Indeed, do not lives destroyed, households uprooted, sorceries, deceptions, desperate straits, and many other evils arise from adultery?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀδιάφορα τίθενται","chosen":"classify ... as matters of indifference","rationale":"ἀδιάφορα is a philosophical term for things considered neither morally good nor morally bad; “morally indifferent” is an equivalent rendering."},{"source_quote":"τῇ φύσει ... θετοῖς ... νόμοις","chosen":"by nature ... by enacted laws","rationale":"Preserves the philosophers’ contrast between what is wrong by nature and what is prohibited only by laws that human beings have laid down. “Conventional laws” is an alternative for θετοῖς νόμοις."},{"source_quote":"εὐριπίστῳ ψυχῇ","chosen":"readily agitated in soul","rationale":"The adjective depicts a soul easily moved or tossed about; “easily swayed in spirit” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς ἀλλήλους πόλεμον αἴρονται","chosen":"go to war against one another","rationale":"The phrase literally describes raising or taking up war and can encompass both organized war and violent conflict."},{"source_quote":"βίων περιγραφαί","chosen":"lives destroyed","rationale":"The phrase can suggest curtailment, destruction, or proscription of lives, while βίοι may also denote livelihoods. The preceding reference to murders favors destruction of lives, though “livelihoods ruined” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"οἴκων ἀναστάσεις","chosen":"households uprooted","rationale":"ἀνάστασις here denotes removal, overthrow, or devastation; “ruin of households” is a less image-preserving alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἀπορίαι","chosen":"desperate straits","rationale":"The plural can denote lack of resources, helpless predicaments, or poverty; the broader rendering fits the list of consequences."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
